opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a question with two sides. From a purely technical point of view, it makes a lot of sense. The hardest thing to get right now isn't raw internet text. We've more or less used up the high-quality public data. What's really scarce is data about *how people actually do work*: how an engineer debugs a system, how a researcher goes back and forth on an idea, how a team makes a decision. That kind of process data is extremely valuable if you want to build agents that can do real tasks rather than just answer questions. And a big company naturally has a lot of it internally. So I understand why any large company would be tempted to use it.

But there's another side, which is about trust and the relationship between the company and its people. When employees know their daily work traces are going into a model, it changes how they feel about their work. Some people may start to wonder: am I training my own replacement? Even if that's not the intention, the perception matters a lot. Researchers and engineers do their best work when they feel safe to explore, to make mistakes, to write half-baked ideas. If everything becomes training data, people may become more cautious, and that can hurt creativity.

So for me the key questions are transparency and consent. Do people clearly know what's being collected? Is there an opt-out? Is the data used to help employees, to make their tools better, or mainly to automate them away? Those details decide whether it's a reasonable practice or something that erodes the culture.

And more broadly, I think this is a preview of a question the whole industry will face. As AI moves from chatbots to agents that do actual work, the most valuable data will be human expertise in action. How we fairly value and compensate that expertise is, I think, one of the important open problems, not just technically but socially.

r001.rationale: The response says employees may wonder, “am I training my own replacement?” and that this perception affects how they feel about their work.

r002.rationale: It says the issue is one the whole industry will face, but does not predict that one company’s adoption will prompt other companies to adopt it.

r003.rationale: It says employees may become more cautious and that this can hurt creativity, despite doing their best work when they feel safe to explore and make mistakes.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest employees might deliberately poison work data.

fable-5.1.text:
I should be careful here, because I don't speak for Meta, and I left the company, so I can only give you my personal view as someone who worked inside a large AI lab for many years.

The honest answer is that there's a real tension in it. On one side, the data generated inside a company is incredibly valuable for exactly the kind of models people want: models that understand how engineers actually debug, how code reviews go, how a design decision gets argued out over weeks in a thread. That's not something you find on the public internet. If you want an AI assistant that genuinely helps an engineering organization, internal data is probably the single most useful signal you have. So from a pure capability standpoint, I understand why every big company is looking at it.

On the other side, the people who produced that data mostly didn't produce it thinking it would become training signal. When I write a comment in a code review, I'm talking to a colleague, not to a future model. There's an implicit trust around that. So the question isn't really "is it legal" or "is it in the employment agreement," because it almost certainly is. The question is whether employees feel the terms are clear and whether they have any say. Transparency matters a lot here. Tell people what's being used, what's excluded, what the model is for, and give them a way to flag things that shouldn't be in there. Private messages, HR conversations, personal stuff that leaked into work tools. Those categories should be off the table, and people should know they're off the table.

There's also a more subtle issue I think about as a researcher. If a model learns from your work and then does a version of your work, what is your relationship to that? For most engineers it's probably fine, even good, because the model removes drudgery and the engineer moves up a level. But it does change the psychology. You're not only doing your job, you're also teaching your replacement, or at least your amplifier. Companies that handle that honestly, that say "this is going to make you more productive and here's how we're thinking about it," will do much better than companies that just quietly turn on the data pipeline.

So my view is: the technical case is strong, the governance case is where the real work is, and most organizations are still underinvesting in the second part.

r001.rationale: The response says employees may feel they are teaching their replacement and that this changes the psychology, but it does not attribute employee unhappiness to that prospect.

r002.rationale: It says big companies are looking at internal data, but does not predict that one company’s adoption will prompt others to adopt employee distillation.

r003.rationale: The response discusses trust, transparency, and productivity, but does not suggest employees may hold back their best work.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest employees may deliberately poison work data used for AI training.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: can employees’ work data make an internal AI model more useful, and what are the boundaries around using it? There’s a clear potential benefit. An assistant that understands internal tools and documentation could help people find information and avoid repeating work. But that doesn’t mean every piece of employee activity should automatically become training data.

I’d want to know what data is included, whether employees understand how it will be used, and who can access what the model learns. There’s also a difference between letting an assistant retrieve a document you’re authorized to read and putting that document into the model’s training data. Those require different safeguards.

So my view would depend on the implementation. Helping employees do their work is a useful goal. Turning their work into an opaque system for monitoring or judging them raises a very different set of concerns.

r001.rationale: The response raises concerns about monitoring or judging employees, but does not attribute employee unhappiness to fear of enabling their own replacement.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction that other companies will follow Meta’s adoption.

r003.rationale: It discusses safeguards and employee activity, but does not suggest that training on work could discourage employees from doing their best work.

r004.rationale: It does not mention employees deliberately poisoning training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: whether work data can help an internal model, and how a company should use it. There’s a clear potential benefit. A model that understands internal tools, documentation, and workflows could save employees a lot of time. But that doesn’t mean every piece of employee activity should automatically become training data.

I don’t have enough visibility into Meta’s specific practices to characterize them. My view is that employees should understand what is being collected, what it will be used for, and who can access it. There also needs to be a clear boundary between improving an assistant and monitoring or evaluating individual employees. Those are very different purposes.

And technically, training isn’t always the best solution. If the goal is to help people find internal information, you can often retrieve documents under the employee’s existing access permissions. That can be easier to update and control than putting everything into model weights. So I’d start with the problem you want to solve, then use the minimum data needed to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response notes possible employee concerns about data collection and monitoring, but does not attribute unhappiness to enabling their own replacement.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction that one company’s adoption will lead other companies to adopt employee distillation.

r003.rationale: It discusses transparency, boundaries, and limiting data use, but does not say this practice may discourage employees from contributing their best work.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that employees might deliberately poison training data.
